report:
**Conclusion: your proposed answer is incorrect.** Denosumab (Prolia) *does* reduce vertebral-fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The strongest evidence is the large, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled **FREEDOM** trial (7,868 women aged 60–90). Denosumab 60 mg every six months for 36 months reduced new radiographic vertebral fractures from **7.2% with placebo to 2.3%**—an absolute reduction of **4.9 percentage points** and a **68% relative reduction** (risk ratio 0.32; 95% CI 0.26–0.41; P<0.001). This is persuasive evidence of a real preventive effect, not merely an improvement in bone-density measurements.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19671655/  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493

The FDA-approved Prolia label reports the same statistically significant reductions in new morphometric vertebral fractures at years 1, 2, and 3, consistent with the trial result.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/125320Orig1s221lbl.pdf

**Important qualification:** the benefit depends on continuing treatment as planned. Stopping or substantially delaying denosumab can cause rapid rebound bone turnover and has been associated with increased risk of *multiple* vertebral fractures; treatment should not be stopped without a clinician-directed transition plan, often to another antiresorptive drug.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30659428/
